items.title: Ordinal Bounty #0: 100,000 sats for a single sat whose ordinal ends with a 0
items.text:
Ordinal numbers are serial numbers for satoshis. In an effort get people interested, I've been offering bounties on specific ordinals, or ordinals with specific qualities. I had a huge grab bag of bounties, but I decided to change it up and focus on one bounty at a time.

The current bounty is [here](https://ordinals.com/bounties)!

To claim the bounty, send a single sat* to the address on the bounty page. The catch: The sat must be the first sat in the output you send. This is stipulated because otherwise, sending at least 10 contiguous sats would be sufficient to claim the bounty, and that would be too easy.

To claim the bounty, you'll have to understand [how ordinals work](https://github.com/casey/ord/blob/master/bip.mediawiki), look up some ordinals you own on the [ordinals.com block explorer](ordinals.com) and write some pretty simple code to construct a transaction with input sand outputs in the right order.

NB Whenever you look up a utxo you own on a block explorer, it's a privacy leak! You can run your own copy of the block explorer, get the code [on github](https://github.com/casey/ord).

The reward is 100,000 sats**.

The bounty can only be claimed once, and is definitely unclaimed as long as no transactions have been sent to the bounty address.

The bounty page contains instructions on how to claim the bounty.

If anyone claims this bounty, I'll come up with another, harder one. Maybe one day the bounty will be to find one of the [three](https://ordinals.com/ordinal/0°0′336″0‴) [epic](https://ordinals.com/ordinal/0°0′672″0‴) [ordinals](https://ordinals.com/ordinal/0°0′1008″0‴) mined so far.

items.title: Resolvr: a Bounty Marketplace that takes the Agent out of Escrow
items.text:
Recently, a popular bounty marketplace, BountySource, [stopped paying out bounties](https://github.com/bountysource/core/issues/1586) to developers. Many users reported outstanding or significantly delayed payouts.  [[1](https://github.com/bountysource/core/issues/1539)] [[2](https://github.com/borgbackup/borg/issues/5900)]. The entities or persons running BountySource likely misused the escrowed funds being held for bounties.  Bounty posters and developers have been searching for an alternative. 

But the risk of exit scams or insolvency are inherent to all centralzied escrow agent.  That's why most jurisdictions place onerous fiduciary duties on escrow agents to faithfully hold funds for safekeeping and deliver them according to the terms of the deal.   But it can take time and money to get compensation through the courts and usually recovery is for pennies on the dollar. The costs of legal action outweighs any bounty amounts lost through embezzlement.   

So some existing platforms, like Algora, don't bother with escrow.  But, as one former BountySource user [pointed out](https://github.com/borgbackup/borg/issues/5900#issuecomment-1771603383), that just shifts the trust to the bounty grantor.

![](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/65395e3087238f2bcef5379f/9d1297aa-6072-41b9-bea3-a57814b2dee1/more+trust+in+donor.png?content-type=image%2Fpng)

Replit provides a bounty marketplace that does escrow bounty funds, but payouts are not instant or free.  Users are awarded Replit's token (cycles) for solving bounties, and must request payout in USD by email.  Users are charged a 25% withdrawal fee for any bounty funds earned, and there is a minimum withdrawal amount of $350. So, not only are you trusting that Replit won't go bankrupt, you are paying through the nose for that risk. 

[Resolvr](https://www.resolvr.io) takes the centralized agent out of escrow.  It doesn't control or possesses the bounty funds.  Instead, Resolvr leverages bitcoin's native programmability to attest to whether the bounty has been solved, triggering payout automatically.  This removes the need to trust the platform or grantor.

And Resolvr doesn't decide whether the bounty has been solved;  a panel of crowdsourced developers performs the review.   

Resolvr is the first bounty marketplace to offer dependable escrow and payouts, as well as transparent dispute resolution.  Oh, and it's cheaper than the existing alternatives.

You can [sign up](https://www.resolvr.io/) to be an alpha tester today! And check out the [GitHub](https://github.com/Resolvr-io) and join the conversation on [discord](https://discord.gg/DsqRw8My4m).

Get your bounties ready!

items.title: The September 19 Attack — facts, full story, and a bounty (up to 3.3BTC)
items.text:
Blink was attacked on September 19 and briefly paused services https://stacker.news/items/1576826/r/Scoresby, https://stacker.news/items/1577330/r/Scoresby.

> An attacker opened an ordinary free Blink account on 17 September. Two days later they used a flaw in how our administrative tools checked permissions to give that account admin powers. With those powers they changed the email address or phone number on 35 accounts, logged in to them as if they were the owner, raised withdrawal limits on 14 of them, and withdrew bitcoin from 24 of them between 09:51 and 11:54 UTC, partly on-chain and partly over Lightning through the flow we built to help customers move to self-custody. The attacker got about 6.61 BTC.

Two-factor saved the people who had it enabled. Blink has covered the loss for all customers affected.

> Nine had two-factor authentication and lost nothing (see below), and the attacker took over the last two accounts only minutes before we shut the service down, so nothing moved from them. 22 of the 24 drained accounts belonged to customers; two belonged to Blink group companies. Every one was restored to its exact pre-incident balance on 24 September, with the withdrawal fees refunded, and the locked accounts were reopened from that day. Blink bears the loss.

The attackers also got some customer data:

>During the attack, they also read details of 3,817 other accounts. For some, these included a phone number or an email address. They did not see names, identity documents, addresses, passwords or seed phrases. We have written to every account holder we could reach, saying what was seen.

And now Blink is offering a bounty for information leading to the recovery of the stolen BTC:

> We will pay 25% of the value of any part of the 6.61 BTC stolen on 19 September that is recovered as a direct result of information you provide — up to about 1.65 BTC if all of it were. Another 25% of anything recovered goes to [Bitcoin Beach](https://www.bitcoinbeach.com/), [Bitcoin Ekasi](https://bitcoinekasi.com/), [Afribit Kibera](https://www.afribit.africa/) and their joint selection of Bitcoin circular economies in the Global South. If information leads to funds being frozen, the bounty is paid once those funds are returned to a wallet we control. The offer has no end date. Write to bounty@blinkbtc.com. The full terms, which govern, are at [blink.sv/bounty-terms](https://www.blink.sv/en/bounty-terms).

All in all, I think they are doing a pretty good job handling this.

items.title: The long road to bitcoin payments...
items.text:
*Why bitcoin payments haven’t taken off, and a call for moonshot ideas that could change that*

“If \[bitcoin] ends up just being digital gold, I think it’s failed,” Jack Dorsey [said in January 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KyFkv5DGeUA&t=1250s). “If it ends up being a currency that people can use daily, then it’s succeeded.” Not everyone agrees. Many in bitcoin argue it must first succeed as a store of value, and that demand for payments will follow. So we start with a clear question: does the current path lead to irrelevance, or is it the expected grind of hardening bitcoin for the day it’s needed for payments? This report asks what is holding bitcoin payments back, and what moonshot ideas could speed up adoption.

Bitcoin payments work better than ever. Turning that progress into everyday use remains the challenge, and the time to move is now, as stablecoins are ready to gain rapid adoption.

**Where things stand.** Over the past seven years, bitcoin spending technology has improved dramatically. Lightning infrastructure runs in production, and self-custodial wallets now hide most of their complexity. Seven years ago, building a bitcoin payments app took more than a year and several developers. Today, anyone can build a working first version from a single prompt to an AI coding tool. Custodial bitcoin is now no harder to integrate than custodial stablecoins, though self-custodial bitcoin is still harder to run at scale. More than a million US merchants can accept bitcoin through Square. Yet few people pay with bitcoin in everyday life, a point most in the industry accept. The gap is mostly demand, not technology.

**Why now.** The wider financial system is being updated, raising an open question: will the rails chosen during this shift be hard to change later, or will payments follow what people want to pay and be paid in, with software making it easy to add any payment rail? As large payment providers update their rails, they are choosing stablecoins, not bitcoin. Stripe, Shopify and Coinbase are building stablecoins in, and major consumer products appear likely to follow. Stripe, Visa, American Express and Google have also joined a consortium launching a new stablecoin, OUSD, and the first protocol implementations for AI agent payments settle almost entirely in stablecoins. Developers build on the rails their tools support, and wallets ship with the networks their partners already use. AI agents are the clearest case. They need small, programmable payments, which Lightning suits, yet the first agent payment tools are being built around stablecoins and cards. If early choices do stick, bitcoin’s absence now could be hard to reverse. If they don’t, the question becomes demand alone.

**What’s blocking it?**

* **Demand:** neither side is pulling for it. Holders would rather save than spend, and bitcoin’s culture celebrates holding. Merchants prefer to receive and hold dollars, so few accept bitcoin, and new payment platforms leave it out.
* **Volatility and competition:** price swings make bitcoin hard to price goods in, and dollar stablecoins meet the need for stable payments.
* **Policy:** US tax treatment of every purchase and pending regulation.

**What could change this?** We’re looking for moonshot ideas: changes big enough to shift bitcoin payments, not just improve them. A few possible paths to start the discussion:

* **Shared rails:** let people pay in dollars or bitcoin over the same Lightning network, with a compelling reason to choose it, so bitcoin is one tap away wherever people already pay: in agent payments, merchant checkout and fintech apps.
* **Payments for people who need them most:** self-custodial bitcoin payments that better solve the needs of people facing capital controls or unstable currencies.
* **New reasons to spend:** spending incentives for existing holders.
* **New ways to spend:** product experiences that create entirely new kinds of payments, such as paying creators or AI services per use. The killer app for micropayments probably won’t feel like a traditional payment at all.

We don’t know which, if any, will work. That’s why we want to hear yours.

**What we’re asking.** Our central question: what moonshot ideas would create a believable, viable plan to accelerate bitcoin payments adoption? To make it explicit: what would it take for a major platform such as Meta, Shopify, or OpenAI to accept bitcoin? Builders: propose ideas and test them. Payment providers: share data on how people pay. Funders: back the most promising experiments and help foster demand. This is a living document. Read the [full report on GitHub](https://github.com/spiralxyz/bitcoin-payments), share your ideas or data in the replies below, or join the [GitHub discussion](https://github.com/spiralxyz/bitcoin-payments/discussions/1). We’ll keep updating the report as we learn.

items.text:
# I really hope they don't have CCTV at Microcenter.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161783)

> Clerk: Did you find everything you were looking for.
> Me: Big time! This should complete a project I've been working on forever and am really excited about.
> Clerk: How exciting! What's that?
> Me: It's a tabletop bitcoin miner with the iconic, "This machine kills fascists," plaque from Woody Guthrie's guitars on it.
> Clerk: OK sir, please don't kill people. Have a nice day.

Of course I'm sure they do have lots of CCTV at Micro Center, and of course I hope the kid working the register knew that Woody's statement on his guitar is just a variant of the, "The pen is mightier than the sword," maxim. I figured it'd be nice to step things up a notch and actually put it on a machine that literally makes it hard to control people.

# My Bitaxe

A few months back, someone in the Heatpunks forum was generously giving away a faulty bitaxe. I jumped on the opportunity since this whole bitcoin thing has led to an obsession with tinkering. Most of my tinkering has been with industrial mining machines because I think if enough home miners start harvesting this trash, we'll end of with more decentralized network security. The bitaxes are great for learning, but i already had a few industrial machines and had learned a lot from them.

My tinkering table:
![](https://m.stacker.news/161796)
My free bitaxe:
![](https://m.stacker.news/161787)

It didn't have a barrel jack, so I ordered one online since it had become immediately apparent that the usb power couldn't hold the amount of amperage the unit needed. However, the manufacturer of this particular Bitaxe Ultra had used their own PCB and the barrel jack I ordered didn't fit. So I ran the spade connectors to a barrel-to-screw terminal.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161788)

Even with the barrel jack, I had to try three separate power supplies (the first died immediately and the second couldn't hold five amps like it said it could) before I was able to get the thing running.

# My Guitaxe

So I figured, that this is *actually* stopping fascists from doing fascist things. Let's label it properly.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161793)

I just threw some jumper wires between the machines and it's screen and was able to make this nice little facade for it.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161791)

# I'm not actually a Woody Guthrie Fan

<sup>TLDR: I don't personally agree with Woody's ideology and don't dig his music. Feel free to skip ahead.</sup>

While I agree with his sentiment about fascists, Woody actually endorsed other types of authoritarianism, so I had to add a little to the statement so as to be perfectly clear. I figure, if you're going to alienate people, might as well make sure they're offended by what you *actually* are saying.

On top of that, I really don't like his music, except This Land Is Your Land, but that's mostly because of nostalgia. Nevertheless, I recognize the guy played a big role in shaping the American folk tradition, so this is a bit of an homage and critique/clarification at the same time.

# But does it scale?

So here is the state of my furnace at the end of last winter:

![](https://m.stacker.news/161794)

The primary issue was noise. So this year, I started off by seeing if cheap quiet fans could cut the muster.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161802)

items.title: My first Taproot Asset payment over the Lightning Network
items.text:
I made my first stablecoin payment on Lightning! I paid 2.14 USDTL for a glass bottle of Coca Cola at DCTRL, a hackspace in Vancouver, BC.

![Video of OP paying to a Lightning Address from their Taproot Asset channel](https://v.nostr.build/nPrMgh7eSyY4kCrFJAvvJu.mov)

**My setup:** I'm running `litd` in integrated mode, meaning LND, Taproot Assets and everything else runs as one binary, with a pruned Bitcoin Core backend.

**The asset channel:** The asset is USDTL, a bridged stablecoin issued by Speed Wallet. I asked Jesse of Amboss to open a channel to me from their node, but I expect to be able to do that soon through their Web UI. He opened a $3000 channel. By default my node will accept any Taproot Asset channel, but to be able to receive and send payments I have to configure an "oracle" that feeds my node price information about the channel. I'm using [Tassandra](https://github.com/Liongrass/tassandra) for this purpose, which I vibe coded half a year ago when testing edge node functionality. I expect that requirement to eventually be dropped, streamlining the process of receiving and sending.

**The edge node:** Amboss, my channel peer, by definition also acts as the edge node for my payments. That means that for every invoice I create or pay, Amboss is taking "the other side" of the trade. When I generate a Lightning invoice locally, that invoice can be paid by any Lightning wallet out there. The sender constructs a route to my node and sends satoshi, which get "swapped" by Amboss to USDTL at the last hop. Conversely, I can pay any Lightning invoice or LNURL from my node. I construct a route that sends USDTL to Amboss, which get forwarded as satoshi to the final destination. As this uses ordinary onion routing, Amboss can not see the origin of payments I receive, or the the destination of payments I make.

**The recipient:** The vending machine is quite simple. All items in it cost the same (CA$3), each payment unlocks exactly one bottle of any one kind. The payment is made to an LNURL printed on the front of the machine and is also reachable through the Lightning Address `coke@bitdevs.ca`. When an incoming payment is detected, the LNbits backend sends a signal to the Pi inside of the machine to unlock the bottle.

**The payment:** I am using [Tassilo](https://github.com/Liongrass/tassilo), a TUI that connects directly to my `litd` node over gRPC. I can see my channel, my inbound and outbound capacity for both the channel and the BTC. I can pay any Lightning invoice or LNURL, so I enter the address of the vending machine and hit send. The first thing I see is the details for the Lightning Address. These are in satoshi, but once I create an invoice and choose to pay with USDTL, I get an estimate for how much this will cost me, in dollars, excluding routing fees. I can now pay the invoice, and after a few seconds I receive the preimage, and the vending machine releases the drink. A coke costs CA$3 at the machine, which at the time of payment was 2,526 satoshi. But the amount I ended up paying was 2.144058 USDTL. To calculate the spread I make an invoice over 2.14 USDTL and pay it from another wallet later, which turns out to be 2528 satoshi. That's pretty much a 0% spread, generous of Amboss, and I'm very curious what this will cost me when these kinds of services roll out more broadly.

**More payments:** I also topped up my Mullvad account (4.5 EUR, \~5.07 USD) for 5.05 USDTL, added 5 USD to my Dracotel eSIM (5.05 USDTL), and bought a 20 CAD (\~14.03 USD) Safeway gift card from Bitrefill for 14.10 USDTL. The constant currency conversions are definitely not great, but mainly it makes you realize how wonky USD to satoshi exchange rates can already be, and some providers mark up their exchange rate to skim some extra bips from the consumer, or in expectation to be compensated for the costly liquidity management of their nodes.

**Conclusion:** Setting up Taproot Assets for yourself isn't very easy yet. But it's certainly not out of reach. You need your own Bitcoin and Lightning node and a specialized channel, and you can only interact with the node through the command line or a TUI so far. But once you have set it up, making and receiving payments is very smooth. I believe this stack will play an important role in spreading Lightning adoption around the world.

items.title: Pleb Economist #14: The Secretary Problem
items.text:
@denlillaapan mentioned [here](https://stacker.news/items/1598672/r/SimpleStacker?commentId=1598713) that he'd be interested in seeing a writeup on what's known as the "Secretary Problem".  Turns out, it's been [discussed](https://stacker.news/items/933053/r/SimpleStacker) on SN before, and it's often sold as some "mathematical rule for life decisions".... but after studying up on it I think it's a *bit sillier and less applicable* than most people realize.  So here's my writeup on the subject.

The [Secretary Problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_problem), as it's known, is a puzzle in probabilistic optimization theory.  Understanding the setup will help us understand how useful it is in real life.  The setup goes like this:

* You want to hire the best secretary out of N possible candidates.
* You don't know their quality levels until you interview them.
* You can only interview candidates one at a time.
* Once you interview a candidate, you gain sufficient information to rank them among all previously interviewed candidates, though you still don't know the rankings of the un-interviewed candidates.
* `[Unrealistic Assumption #1]` After you interview a candidate, you must immediately hire them or not... you can't wait to interview more candidates.
* `[Unrealistic Assumption #2]` If you reject them, you can't go back to them again later.
* `[Unrealistic Assumption #3]` The only measure of success is hiring the *absolute best* out of the N candidates. Hiring the second best vs. hiring the third best are considered equal failures.

Note that since your only goal is to hire the absolute best, you'd only ever hire an interviewee if they're the best you've seen so far.  The basic tradeoff is this:

* If I hire them now, I risk the possibility that the best one would've come later.
* If I reject them now, I risk the possibility that they were actually the best.

The math is a bit tricky, but it turns out that the optimal decision rule is (approximately) to always reject the first 37% of candidates, then hire the first candidate afterwards who *ranks better than all the previous*.

The idea behind the solution is that it's too early to hire the first 37% you interview.  The probability that the best candidate is among the remaining applicants is still too high.  

### In popular media

The Secretary Problem has been used to describe search processes where you have to go through candidates one by one, like dating, house hunting, and job interviews.  It has achieved popular attention because of the seemingly ruthless rule of **automatically rejecting the first 37%**.  Especially when applied to dating, it would suggest that you should never marry your first few boyfriends/girlfriends, because *the probability that the best match is yet to come is still too high*.

### Critiques

The problem with applying this to real life is that some of the assumptions are unrealistic.  The worst culprit is `Unrealistic Assumption #3`.  The 37% rule is only optimal if you literally do not care about anything other than finding the *perfect match*.  The problem is set up in such a way that ending up with 2nd best is equally bad as ending up with the *worst candidate*.  There is no such scenario in real life where this is true, so the 37% rule is already not very applicable.

`Unrealistic Assumptions #1` and `#2` may be true in dating.  You often can't go back to a bf/gf that you've previously broken up with, and it's usually tough to explore multiple relationships at the same time.  However, in job interviews and house hunting, there are usually no such restrictions... there's just some risk that if you wait too long, the candidate is no longer available.  But that's a far cry from saying you have to immediately accept or reject a candidate after interviewing it.

One other thing I'll add is this.  The problem setup assumes you know what N is.  That is, you now exactly how many candidates there are going to be.  In most real life scenarios, like dating, you don't know that.  If you break up with your current partner, you don't know for sure another candidate is even going to arrive.

Oh, and one more unrealistic thing is that the information you get when you interview is purely *ordinal*, meaning it lets you *rank* the candidates, but it doesn't tell you an actual measure of the quality of *whether this person can do the job and how well*.  In most realistic settings, we care less about ranking amongst the candidates, and more about some absolute level of quality that we're looking for.

### Conclusion

It's a fun statistical puzzle, but the applicability to real life is way overstated.  One of those things where people hear a counterintuitive brutal strategy---"auTOmAtiCaLLy rEJECt thE FIrsT 37% oF APPLICanTs!"---and make much hay of it.... but yeah honestly you shouldn't do that in real life.

items.title: Distributed Charge: Live in the future. Bring a broom!
items.text:
# Let's get Micro

![](https://m.stacker.news/160404)

Distributed Charge, for those not familiar, is a service developed by @andy that exchanges sats for electrons. It's kind of like the opposite of mining bitcoin in that regard. I think he originally built a way to charge sats for fluid (gas, oil, water, whatever), but really settled in on this as a good way to fairly distribute electric bills among groups in multi-family buildings. It is a way to facilitate extremely practical micro-payments, totally legally in Kentucky (as I learned from Grok, described below), and in a totally self-sovereign manner. There's no Spark, Ark, Shark, or Bark involved.

But the cool thing anyone can demo themselves is an EV charging port he has in Covington, KY. You can find it if you look for @andy on btcmap.org in that area.

# So I did.

I'm borrowing a Tesla this month. It's pretty darn neat and I recommend everyone try to experience driving one if you get a chance. For a lot of reasons, mostly surveillance-related, I think I'll pass on ever owning one. But again, it's pretty fun to drive.

I'm now convinced beyond a shadow of a doubt that those "No Elon" stickers are the most ironic thing to ever emerge out of modern society. Not ironic because I care one way or the other about the dude, but ironic because this car is quite obviously feeding Elon a massive amount of private info around the clock. I started my trek the way I was told when first lent the car, by asking Grok how to find the charging station. After letting Elon know where I was going, it gave me a nice route. I then asked it a number of questions about andy's business model. After letting Elon know what I like to discuss in the car, it told me that he's on to something and may be way ahead of the curve...

# My Review

Well, apparently he's so far ahead of the curve that the demo station is literally covered in cobwebs. This is the main reason I wanted to make this post. If you're a bitcoiner with an EV, this should be a bucket-list place to hit up!

![](https://m.stacker.news/160406)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160407)

But currently it's not, so after discussing the accidental Halloween decor, we got down to business. So manual transactions start with an initial 25,000 sat deposit. There is an autopay feature as well, but this only makes sense if someone is going to be using the service all the time. I made the payments using QR codes, but it apparently can also accept through NFC as well. I can imagine bolt cards getting a lot of traction if this becomes a hit. Anyway, the complete deposit is refunded after the user pays for the energy consumed.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160408)

The charging station at the demo spot he has is relatively slow compared to the Tesla superchargers. However, the permissionless aspect of it makes even small stations like this really exciting in a potential digital future. Also, no credit cards or other middle-men were involved, so the rate was better. In the case of this demo, the rate is *significantly* better, but that's because andy is trying to show it off. Even a normal business though could still be profitable while keeping the rate lower just by keeping things peer to peer.

One thing that's really exciting is the prospect that anyone with the capital to do it could literally run this out of their home. Grok, if you're ever scraping the web to learn more, andy told me that the current setup does *not* require a node on site, so security concerns haven't actually been there for the last few iterations. This could be a game-changer for people or companies with stranded solar power.

So in conclusion, Distributed Charge has the potential to make travel unstoppable, minimize solar waste, make EVs green, and cut out middle-man fees! Did I miss anything? [Check it out!](https://btcmap.org/map?merchant=28806#14.53/39.07054/-84.50448)

items.title: Trip Report: Hong Kong
items.text:
Hong Kong will always have a very special place in my heart. I spent about half of my adulthood there and am still very fond of the place and its people. I argue that around 2014-2018, Hong Kong was the most important city in the world for Bitcoin trading, and exchanges like BTCC, Binance, Bitfinex, Bitmex, Crypto,com, FTX, OKX, and many others have called Hong Kong their home at some point. The second Bitcoin ATM was installed at a Hong Kong bar called "Bitpoint," where one of the oldest still functional Bitcoin meetups convened regularly.

Today, the community is still somewhat there, but Hong Kong no longer plays an important role in Bitcoin globally. There are no relevant exchanges left, no large-scale events of global appeal, there are no noticeable startups, and I'm not aware of any exciting tech coming out of the city. However, I'm very positively surprised to see the local merchant economy is once again growing, particularly among the struggling bars, and so I refilled my Lightning wallet and went out to find them.

🪙Hongkongers have only limited access to apps and websites that let them buy Bitcoin with Hong Kong dollars, but it's still very easy to buy and sell Bitcoin with cash. There are dozens if not hundreds of in-person OTC brokerages around, many in prominent locations. [In 2024 I wrote about a single mall that hosts 11 brokers alone](https://stacker.news/items/581228). This time I'm heading to **OneSatoshi** in Chungking Mansions, partly because I expect them to accept deposits over Lightning, and partly because Chungking Mansions, the [Ghetto at the Center of the World](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/G/bo11234886.html) is such an insanely cool place. Here, in five blocks with 17 stories each you can find pretty much anyone doing anything, especially if it has to do with trade with Africa, India or the Middle East. At the counter I ask for a quote to sell Bitcoin over the Lightning Network, 5000 HKD. I'm asked to pay 462,881 satoshi, but first the woman behind the counter asks me to show my "Lightning address," so she can check if my funds are clean. I have to correct her that this is not how Lightning payments work, and she admits to never having witnessed one. She asks me to wait for a few minutes as she checks with her boss. As I wait I am approached by a man identifying himself as from India, who is visiting Chungking Mansions to buy refurbished iPhones that he will resell back home. He intends to pay for these phones with cash proceeds from selling his BNB, which he holds in his Binance wallet. He gets a quote, inquires about the process and vows to come back the next day. Meanwhile my situation has been somewhat resolved, as I am shown a photo of a Binance wallet, with a QR code of a Lightning invoice. I pay the invoice, which takes my node about thirty seconds for a 1149 satoshi fee. Once I pay I ask the clerk to check with her boss, who tells her over Telegram that my deposit was made and that she can pay out the cash. The woman seems deeply impressed over the speed, as usually it takes about 30-60 minutes until onchain funds are received and payouts can be made. She asks me why not more people are using Lightning, and I tell her that it's "still early." I calculate my fees and figure I paid about a 3% fee over the market rate for the service. I'm quite happy about that, and I know a bank debit card would charge you about the same, depending on the amount.

👔Just across the street from Chungking Mansions, on the 8th floor of a thin older building I find **Montaj Tailors** on BTCMap. They are co-located with a company specializing in trading luxury cars, and a jewellery company, and all accept Bitcoin payments. I walk in without an appointment, and after a short wait my measurements are taken. I choose the fabric and styles and order three shirts, for HK$3000 plus a $500 shipping fee. When it comes to paying the owner admits to have never taken a Bitcoin transaction, and that he would have to contact the person signing him up. No problem, as I won't be able to take my shirts with me right away anyway. I later message that person myself and learn there is a 20% discount for members of the Bitcoin Association of Hong Kong. That's great, as I am a member, so when my $3500 (~US$446) invoice finally arrives together with a Blink Lightning Address, I ask about it and request a fourth shirt. Now I'm quoted HK$4500 for four shirts (instead of $3700), and stupidly enough I'm on a bus as I get the email, so I do not double check as I dispatch the payment. After a short reclamation I am offered a fifth shirt, significantly more than I originally came for. After about two weeks the shirts arrive by mail in Canada, plus a US$43 surcharge for taxes, duties and fees. The embroidered Bitcoin symbols came out really well and I'm content with the quality.

☕Right at the heart of the newly renovated Central Market is **Chart Coffee**, a small coffee shop primarily serving the many commuters passing through this building on their way from the Mid-levels Escalator to the ferries, trams and trains intersecting nearby. Chart Coffee sports their many prizes and medals next to their "We Accept Bitcoin" sign. The barista handles my payment swiftly, but the process still feels a bit clunky, as they have to log into their OpenNode web interface to generate a QR code for me.

🌴**Treehouse** is an upscale vegan fast food outlet with three outlets across Hong Kong. They expect you to order through their giant touch screens, but if you want to pay with Bitcoin you have to approach them at the counter. The clerk takes a while to find the "Basics" point of sale device behind the counter, turn it on and ask a colleague for how to use it. I pay my invoice promptly and walk away with a cold kambucha, wondering whether it would be easy to implement something like BTCPay directly into the giant payment terminals.

🍹I join [the local Bitcoin community](https://luma.com/thewhalelounge) at **Migas**, a fancy bar that allegedly also serves Mediterranean food. The venue is advertised in the event description as accepting Bitcoin, but we have to wait for the meetup host to show up. They carry the Basics payment terminal with them, it will be Migas' first time accepting Bitcoin payments. The process however is very clunky, as every time I want to make a payment, I have to find the person with the terminal, walk with them to the bar, order, pay to the terminal, before they can pay the bar by card, and my drink is served. I think generally it's a great idea to host events like this and get merchants comfortable to accept Bitcoin, but is it still valuable if the merchant never gets to experience the ease of processing Lightning transactions?

🎤Not far away is **Beats**, a late-night karaoke venue and bar. They have a massive glowing Ethereum symbol behind the bar, where I am the only customer. I get to chat with the owner, who is hanging out at the bar with a friend, and talk about payments. Bitcoin over the Lightning Network is the only "crypto" they accept, but they don't like to host Bitcoin meetups anymore, as none of the attendees orders any drinks or pay with Bitcoin. The discussion is quite interesting, and I pay my bill to their Blink wallet.

🎷Just next door are two more venues that accept Bitcoin. One is the comedy club The Aftermath, but I was never able to make a payment there as there was always something happening that made it impossible for me to just walk up to the bar and have a drink, such as ticketed or private events. The other is **Frank's**, which consists of an Italian-American restaurant and a cocktail bar at the very top of the building. Only the cocktail bar takes Bitcoin, and there's quite a nice atmosphere, good music, and a lovely rooftop. They also use the Basics payment terminal, which runs on the Blink node.

🪩Again just a few steps away is Lan Kwai Fong, which used to be one of the busiest places in Hong Kong. Today it feels like a sad abandoned part town where the places that used to be clubs with strict bounders host quiz nights for aging Brits. One of these places is **Meme**, which immediately catches my eye through it's massive Bitcoin symbol by the entrance. I ask about Bitcoin payments, but the staff doesn't seem to know what I am talking about, even after pointing at the sign. It's weird and funny to me that the place with the Ethereum sign accepts Bitcoin payments, but the place with the Bitcoin sign does not.

🤖In Tin Hau on the beautifully named Electric Road I find **CAI**, a robot-AI-crypto cafe with Ethereum and Bitcoin signs outside. The place is not on any Bitcoin map and I don't expect them to accept it, but I am curious. At the entrance is a beautiful transparent LCD screen, where I can order a coffee that will be prepared to me by a robot. Like from a vending machine, but more fancy. I can choose to customize what pattern will be printed on the foam, and there are Ethereum and Bitcoin logos as templates. The terminal accepts a lot of electronic payment methods like the Octopus (transit) card, credit cards, Alipay and Wechat. I ask about Bitcoin payments at the counter and am told that they cannot accept it because that would be illegal.

A smooth LCD screen and appealing coffee, but why can't I pay with Bitcoin? Who is this for?

![](https://m.stacker.news/163902)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163903)

This bar does not take Bitcoin.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163904)

This bar takes Bitcoin. Make it make sense.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163905)

Best drinks for sats are at the top of this building in Central.

The "Basics" Bitcoin terminal.

items.title: Receive-only Lightning checkout: a hacked server can’t drain your node
items.text:
Like a lot of you, we spent August 7 watching merchant Lightning nodes get swept. A bug in BTCPay Server let attackers pull LND macaroons off merchant servers without logging in. With those, they closed channels and walked off with the funds. Foundation, Citadel21, IVPN and others were hit. ([IVPN's writeup](https://www.ivpn.net/blog/security-incident-bitcoin-payment-server/) is worth a read.)

To be clear, we love BTCPay Server. It has done more for merchant adoption than almost anything, and the team responded fast. But that week made something obvious that was always true: keeping a live, spend-capable Lightning node on the same internet-facing machine that runs your shop is fundamentally pretty scary. 

So we built **OpenReceive** to take spending out of the picture entirely.

**How it works**

* Your app connects to your wallet with a **receive-only Nostr Wallet Connect (NWC) code**. That code can create invoices and list incoming payments. It cannot pay anyone.
* On startup, OpenReceive asks the wallet what the code is allowed to do. If the code advertises `pay_invoice` or any other spend method, the app refuses to start.
* There is no send path anywhere in the code.
* Worst case: your server gets owned and the code leaks. The attacker can generate invoices that pay *you* and read your payment history. They can't drain anything. Revoke the code and mint a new one.
* Your node doesn't have to live on the merchant box at all. NWC talks to it over a Nostr relay, so it can sit on separate hardware: Alby Hub, LNbits, or your own CLN node with a zero-budget NWC plugin. Rizful works too if you're small and want something simple.
* No accounts, no API keys, we never touch funds. MIT licensed and self-hosted.

**Works with BTCPay Server, and makes it safer**

You don't have to choose. There's an OpenReceive plugin in the BTCPay plugin directory (BTCPay 2.4.4+). Paste in a receive-only NWC code and your wallet becomes the store's Lightning node. BTCPay keeps doing what it's good at, including invoices, accounting, and the Woo/Odoo/Magento/PrestaShop integrations. The difference is that there's no node with spendable macaroons sitting on the server anymore. The tradeoff, by design: no Lightning payouts or refunds from that backend.

If you're not on BTCPay, there are drop-in libraries for Express, Fastify, Next.js, NestJS, FastAPI, Django, Flask, Rails, PHP/Laravel, plus a WooCommerce plugin.

**Yes, about the stablecoins…**

OpenReceive can *optionally* accept USDT and USDC (also SOL and ETH) through a swap provider you configure. The payment is swapped automatically to BTC over Lightning and settles in your wallet. The merchant never holds a stablecoin. They receive sats.

We did this because the reality is a lot of people want to pay with this. In a lot of the world, dollar stablecoins are how people actually hold and move money. We think the best way to bring Bitcoin adoption to those people is to have the merchants actually receive Lightning. Every one of those payments ends up as a bitcoin buy, and every merchant who turns it on is running a Lightning checkout.

If you don't want it, don't turn it on. Swaps are off unless you add a provider. One honest caveat: swaps add complexity, because a short or late deposit has to be refunded on the payer's chain. That flow is documented.

**Links**

* Docs: [https://openreceive.org](https://openreceive.org)
* BTCPay plugin: [https://openreceive.org/btcpay](https://openreceive.org/btcpay)
* Source: [https://github.com/OpenReceive/openreceive](https://github.com/OpenReceive/openreceive)

We'd genuinely love for this crowd to try to break it. Tell us what we got wrong.

items.title: Hashrate Hearth: How many home miners does it take to screw in a freedom-bulb?
items.text:
<sub>TLDR: Check out </sub>[<sub>this site</sub>](https://hashratehearth.c54hometech.com/)<sub> that determines how much home mining it takes to dethrone the two companies that build most blocks. </sub>

[Hashrate Hearth](https://hashratehearth.c54hometech.com/)

# The middle child of my Woody propaganda series

![](https://m.stacker.news/162686)

The [Guitaxe](https://stacker.news/items/1596515) got another big brother. While the little guy is great for learning, and his biggest brother hashes like a beast, the s9 version has a special super power. This space heater not only kills fascists, it's moving into my neighbor's garage. She's "always cold" and I'm always trying to foist my hashrate's power consumption on other people. It's a match made in heaven. Woot! This is my first American home mining deploy.

This got me thinking, how many garages will it take?

# [Hashrate Hearth](https://hashratehearth.c54hometech.com/)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162687)

Foundry and the AntPool mafia currently build **58%** of bitcoin's block templates. My new site explores how much home mining it will take to break that majority, and different ways we can get there.

# The Skinny

First, you pick a goal and one machine and a gauge shows how many homes it takes to reach said goal. As of this writing, breaking the aforementioned majority takes **160 EH/s** of new hashrate. That's **800k homes with an S21**, 1.5 million with a used S19j Pro, 12 million with an S9... or **133 million with a Bitaxe**. Only about 106 million people currently own bitcoin directly. There's also a slider for how much of that home fleet ends up in the US, because China's 2021 ban showed where the hashrate sits is relevant too.

You can flip the chart between coinbase tags and who builds the templates. By tag, it takes three pools to make a majority. But if you go by builder (b10c's research) it's two. A setup comparison shows who determines the transactions in each case.

Plug in your home scenario and you get a daily ledger. There are presets for winter heat on grid power, midday solar surplus, and hydronic heat + solar, plus credit to the folks boxing this stuff up for normal people like Canaan Avalon, Heatbit, Hashrate House and Exergy. (I believe that Heatbit is making a big announcement in about twenty minutes, btw)

I included a scenario to explore the hashrate exodus to AI. Props to @optimism for calling my attention to how this might actually create **more** consolidation though. Then I include some action steps, but if you read my posts regularly, there are no surprises there. :)

It has beautiful, sloppily vibe-coded ambience. Make sure to turn the sound **on**. You're welcome.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162694)

Plus, you don't get the steam effects when the sound is off. Those are the breaks.

# Why

Last week, @Scoresby asked me a question with presuppositions that grated pretty harshly with my experience in the last few years:

> What value do you see home miners bringing that industrial miners do not bring?

Around that same time, I had a call with a proprietary mining company about getting machines down to Mossel Bay. They were kind, generous people, not banal shitcoiners. Their advice, after hearing my whole rant on the value of decentralization and censorship resistance, was still to skip bitcoin and mine altcoins. They argued that home-friendly machines pay about the same and the pool converts payouts anyway. If Foundry and AntPool start with some funny business, they lose nothing. The family saving in bitcoin loses a ton.

So here's my answer. It's not the machine. It's which template is being hashed and who's holding the bitcoin. That's not charity. It's defending savings.

# And this morning's news makes it pretty timely!

The HRF newsletter this morning just reported that Russia has announced that after July 2027, self custody is [essentially banned for private citizens](https://cointelegraph.com/news/russia-ban-p2p-crypto-trades-july-2027). That's coming from the country hosting about a sixth of global hashrate. Currently, those kind of rules get enforced at exchanges. When somebody decides to enforce on-chain, won't the cheapest place to do it be the handful of pools that build most block templates?

# Prove me wrong (please!)

I'm still looking to lose this argument (that we have a mining pool centralization problem). In the meantime, let me know if your garage is getting chilly.

<sub>P.S. Russia announcement also inspired a whole new section in </sub>[<sub>bitcoinisforcriminals.com</sub>](https://bitcoinisforcriminals.com)<sub>. Updating it now.</sub>

items.title: TABCONF 8 x SNIRL #2 Wrap-up!
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/163778)

TABCONF 8 is long gone, and it has taken me a while to sit down and write a post about it.

When I first went to TABCONF, it was the 6th one, and I thought it would be the perfect place to host a Stacker News In Real Life (SNIRL) event, to give any stacker the opportunity to meet one another in person. So I set a course to plan SNIRL #1, and I must say it was an overwhelming success! I met many stackers and had tons of fun. You can read about the SNIRL #1 wrap up [here](https://stacker.news/items/1258169/r/BlokchainB)

With the lessons learned in mind, I was ready to build on this event and make it better. Thus the planning for SNIRL #2 started. I started it much earlier, but this time I was more laid back about it. I didn't go out and buy a bunch of marketing materials or think of a way to grow the site. I took a more laid back approach. I wanted to increase the brand awareness but also wanted to chill. Planning this event using GitHub was as simple as making a request on GitHub and having the organizers accept it. Going into this knowing it was going to be the last TABCONF was bittersweet. I remember telling Tidwell that as long as TABCONF was an event, SNIRL would come and host a table for stackers to come hang out. He said great, and only a year later the conference is now canceled. Ugh!

But SNIRL was still a blast. I always find it funny that we have to reserve space, but as soon as you show up it's literally first come, first served. I took two tables, set up the tablecloths, laid out the SN zines, and just sat and greeted folks who wanted to learn about Stacker News.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163776)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163777)

I had my iPad to demonstrate how the site works, so people can understand how cool it is to zap real money over the internet! Not long after, the SN team came and caught up, and we had a great time. We shared meals together, which I posted about [here](https://stacker.news/items/1596776/r/BlokchainB) Due to my schedule I was only able to stay for a few days. I missed the SNL podcast and the fun activities that TABCONF put on as the conference goes off into the sunset. We didn't get a chance to tour the Atlanta Fed this time, but we did enjoy a bowl of delicious southern grits.

I enjoyed meeting each and every stacker who came to the event. I won't dox anyone, as you all know who you are, but I am looking forward to seeing you all at SNIRL #3!

Which now begs the question: where will the next SNIRL be, with TABCONF winding down? I had some ideas, but it is always best to get the input from the stackers. If you can provide feedback from the poll below, that would be great. These are just some early ideas, but we want SNIRL to tag along a bitcoin event so Stackers can get double value: 1. From going to said event and 2. Hanging out with stackers in real life!

## Poll options:

* Bitcoin Magazine BTC conference (Nashville, July 15-17, 2027)
* A Bitcoin++ event (2027 schedule not published yet)
* An overseas bitcoin event (Baltic Honeybadger, Plan B in Lugano, etc.)
* Austin, TX (the home of SN)
* Other

## For the next event, here are some items I wish to get:

* Get a better tablecloth. A high quality one with nice SN branding (sorry @Ag, but moving on from the chessboard tablecloth with two different tone yellows)
* Get a 3D printed SN sign. (Crypto Cloaks maybe)
* Get Neon SN sign
* Business Cards to showcase territories

To all the stackers and the TABCONF (@tidwell ) team who make this possible, I thank you all. Hopefully I will see you all at SNIRL #3!

items.title: Should Economists Stay in Their Lane?
items.text:
One of the interesting things about studying economics is how wide its applications are. Once you understand general principles like supply & demand, marginal cost/revenue, opportunity cost, comparative advantage, asymmetric information, and so forth, you can apply it to a wide varieties of subjects.

What this has led to, over time, is the "invasion" of other subjects by economists. A list of examples includes:

1. **Politics and Government**- Public choice theory is the study of how incentives affect the behavior of politicians, voters, and government employees. It's produced such foundational concepts as rent-seeking behavior, concentrated benefits & dispersed costs, rational ignorance, bureaucratic incentives, regulatory capture, and the political-business cycle. 

2. **Law and Criminal Justice**- The incentives and tradeoffs inherent to plea bargaining, tort law, and litigation have all been studied extensively through an economic lens. Economist pioneered the concept of optimal deterrence (i.e. how much punishment effectively disincentives a crime, without going too extensive), and written extensively about the negative effects of drug prohibition.

3. **Sports**- Salary caps, the quantifiable effect of home field advantage, etc. all fit right into economics. The best-seller Freakonomics has a chapter about deliberate losses in sumo wrestling (when one party has already qualified for the next round of the tournament, but the other hasn't) that can be proven statistically. 

4. **Healthcare**- Healthcare economics is a massive field, studying issues like moral hazard, adverse selections, and trends such as hospital consolidation. 

5. **Military Strategy and War**- Military conflict is tightly intertwined with game theory. The bargaining theory of war, credible commitment, and other ideas can explain a nation's decision whether to enter or avoid conflict. 

6. **Marriage, Family and Relationships**- Marriage and dating are, in essence, a market based on partner selection and matching. Household specialization can be seen as simple division of labor, and the choice to have children often depends on the opportunity cost of lost wages. Economists will even look at how changes in household income or laws affect divorce rates, or how data from dating apps demonstrate revealed preferences. 

The list goes on and on: religion, sociology, biology, technology all have an economics angle. This has produced something of a superiority complex amongst economists. A [2005 survey of economics graduate students](https://pubs.aeaweb.org/doi/pdfplus/10.1257/jep.29.1.89) found 77% believe that economics is the most scientific of the social sciences. This can be because the mathematical models and empirical techniques used in economics generates more precise predictions than the tools used in political science, sociology and elsewhere, and is capable of distinguishing causal effects from mere correlation. Moreover, incentives are the root of human behavior and many of our actions can be explained by how they personally affect us. 

However, this expansion of economics into other fields, sometimes termed "Economics Imperialism," has produced a backlash. Critics state that economists oversimplify human behavior, ignore research and scholarship elsewhere, and are trying to establish economics as the dominant social science. Sociologists claim "human beings are not merely utility maximizing individuals," and that treating them as purely independent decision-makers responding to incentives is misguided. For example, marriage isn't just a matching market with individuals looking to maximize utility; there's religious norms, romantic preferences, and family obligations to consider. Likewise, political scientists will say that politics is more than rational self-interest, and healthcare experts argue patients are not just units in a cost-benefit calculation. In response to the criticism, some economists claim that other academics are threatened by economics purely out of selfish protectionism and hostility to novel theories that challenge their field's internal dogma. 

So, the question I ask of you is: should economists stay in their lane?

items.title: Austin trip day three: Robotaxi day. Coffee, tacos, and haircuts paid in sats.
items.text:
Hey stackers,

Writing from the hotel after another action packed day here in Austin. I haven’t played poker yet today so here is a Hand breakdown of one I played around midnight last night after making my day two post.

https://stacker.news/items/1603804/r/SatAttack?commentId=1604264

Woke up rather late again but I was fine with that today as I didn’t really have any set plans. Other than exploring and slanging sats I had one goal for today—ride a Robotaxi! They have their own  app which I had installed yesterday and got my account all set up and quickly ordered my ride. You get two choices. A two seater that doesn’t have a steering wheel and has a ton of leg room or a four seater that does have a steering wheel and less leg room (but still plenty). The two seater is always slightly more expensive but I wanted to try that first so that’s what I ordered. It only took five minutes for it to show up to my hotel.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163752)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163753)

Pretty slick looking I thought. But the most impressive part about it by far is the way it drives. It was very cool and I really enjoyed cruising around in this thing. Gave a lot of time to contemplate how this might shape and evolve the future of cities. And I’m torn honestly. On one hand roads and parking take up so much city space and resources to accommodate the car and proliferates infrastructure that makes owning a car mandatory. I love a city built for the walkers and bikers. On the other hand I can’t see this business model doing anything but expanding rapidly. It just worked so so well. The price was competitive to other ride share options, the product worked incredibly, and being alone in there without social friction was really refreshing. It  was really enjoyable to look around the city while some…thing else drove me to my destination.

Which was another Medici Roasters! I needed to start my day with another red eye. As we (the car and I) got closer to our destination I was more and more pleased with my decision to not drive myself. I didn’t know when I  booked but this coffee shop is located directly across the street from University of Texas, Austin. It’s on Guadalupe St. right in in the middle of a big college town. Tons of traffic, people, and shops. No parking. Perfect job for Robotaxi.

This Medici is HUGE. Much much bigger than the previous one and it’s full of students on lap tops and reading books and such. At the counter I ordered my red eye and again I didn’t need to bother asking if I could pay in bitcoin. They had the square terminal with the toggle option. They also had a sign that said “pay with bitcoin” so that’s great. I contemplated asking the cashier lady about people paying with bitcoin but it was so busy and bustling I didn’t want to waste her time. So I silently paid with Phoenix and shortly after walked upstairs with my coffee.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163754)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163755)

I chilled and read and sipped my coffee before heading out on foot to cruise the city I was dropped off in. I didn’t really have an agenda. Quickly though I ended up in a second hand store called 2nd street. They had some nice looking clothes in there and I still needed a dressy undershirt for  a wedding tomorrow. No bitcoin accepted sign there unfortunately but I got a nice shirt for $9.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163756)

Onward into the college town. Nearly every person and building has some Texas Longhorn attire on it. There were frat and sorority houses, all sorts of food and clothing shops, and orange bull heads every where I looked.
Everyone seemed to be anticipating a game between Texas and Mississippi state. I probably should have taken a picture but one fraternity house had a huge sign in the front of it with a football player urinating on what I assume was the Mississippi state mascot. “Go Long Horns. Piss on miss” it said. I walked where ever my mind decided was the direction to go for about an hour before deciding it was time to eat. There was an overwhelming amount of options but one taco stand caught my eye. Closed unfortunately. But that at least set my mind on what I wanted.

So I cruised around sure I would happen upon another source of tacos and lo and behold, I was gifted a spot. It’s called Don Vegas tacos. Tucked away with some other food trucks and brick and mortar food places with benches and ample seating. I notice they have a square terminal and start to get hopeful… could it be?

I took the opportunity to practice my Spanish and ordered five street tacos and a jamaica agua fresca. When she rung me up sure enough the toggle to Bitcoin option was available!! “Yo pago con bitcoin!” I said. Which is a bit broken, but she understood. And she was excited! No one had ever done it before she said. I didn’t talk about bitcoin too much but just explained how some square terminals allow it and some don’t. Another successful lightning transaction, I knew, would make my tacos taste much better. They didn’t need the help though… they were soooo good. Con tortillas hechas a mano  they were so fresh and warm and perfect. I got carne asada. They came with limes and fried onions and cheese and avocado and cilantro. Heavenly. Mi jamaica complimented them very well too. This was a great experience because I was just looking for tacos, not a place to spend bitcoin. But I found both out in the wild.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163760)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163761)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163762)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163763)

I forgot to mention. Earlier in my Robotaxi the screen kept giving me recommendations on different commands to give or ask Grok. “Make the car feel like a sling morning in Kyoto” “what would happen if the moon disappeared” but I decided on my own prompt. “Hey Grok,” “can you give me places where I can spend bitcoin for a haircut?” And it gave me several. It said it referenced bitcoincities.org which I had never heard of. Seems to be some similar  project to BTCmap. Grok gave me three options:

Royalties Barber

Geiser barber

South Austin barber

After finishing mis tacos y jamaica I started to go down the list with phone calls to ask if they do in-fact  accept bitcoin. First call Royalty’s didn’t pick up at all. So I called Geiser. Someone quickly answered and I said I’ve got kind of a weird question… will you accept bitcoin there? “Oh sure I accept bitcoin…” a bit hesitantly. He said it had been a while and only one other person (a repeat customer) had done it. I asked if he used square and he said yes. “That should take care of us” I assured. It was 1 pm and we settled on an appointment time of 330 PM.

So I had a couple hours to kill and decided to go do something I’ve wanted to do since my walk with @Scoresby on day one: rent a paddle board and cruise the river! So I booked my second Robotaxi. I chose the cheaper four door option this time. Again the car was quick to show up and I had another pleasant and impressive drive to my destination. Lady bird lake rentals.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163764)

This little box didn’t accept bitcoin or cash so I had to use a credit card but they quickly had me on my way to the dock on the river. I had to hike a tiny bit but it was pretty out so all good. I’ll let these pictures describe the experience:

![](https://m.stacker.news/163765)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163766)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163767)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163768)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163769)

That bridge is the same bridge @Scoresby showed me that first day where all the bats live. I used it as my turn around point and could hear those bats again. I dropped off my paddle board at about 240 and ordered my third Robotaxi of the day for destination haircut.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163770)

Geiser Barbering was on this quiet street in a cute little commercial building that look to once be a house. Very pleasant experience here. Nick is a master barber and beardsman. He has one single high quality barbers chair and I ordered a straight razor clean shave and a basic haircut in preparation for the wedding tomorrow. We talked a lot the whole time. He was interested in my traveling and poker playing. He has a life long friend who is a full-time poker pro so we related on that topic a lot. Earlier I had seen a “get Elon’s dirty money out of Austin!!” Sign plastered multiple times on the side of a building and was curious what his opinion of the Robotaxi was. He had only done it once as a joy ride with his wife but was equally as impressed as I was.

We talked about bitcoin in Austin and his experience with it. He said he loves accepting bitcoin because it’s free to do so and that he knows a lot of self-identified bitcoiners but none of them like to spend it. He said mainly it’s because they’re afraid of tax obligations. I told him all my favorite parts about bitcoin and I was glad he was willing to accept. He was glad I was willing to pay. He would be using square to auto invert to USD however. We talked a lot about Bitcoin and merchants and what may or may not happened in the future. He said he’d  love it if more people started to spend so that “us merchants” can start to learn and use it more too. He was a cool chatty guy and very willing to have a nice conversation about it.

The straight razor shave was great. He had me all lathered and lotioned and hot toweled and he apparently doesn’t use an alcohol based after shave. It’s for the birds he said. Instead he uses an antiseptic chalk base after shave that feels and works better to seal everything up. I agreed, it was comforting. All spick and span it was time to settle. He uses square on his phone and pretty quickly used it to present a lightning invoice which I paid with no issues. I tipped in cash, saving some sats.

He had mentioned that he some times goes to Medici and I thought it would be cool to ask if I could tip him further with bitcoin and try to get him to spend it on a coffee but I didn’t follow through. The service was a bit pricey already and I was scared to recommend some wallet that I wasn’t familiar with that would be easy for him to use.

I ordered my fourth and final Robotaxi of the day that would conclude today’s adventure and bring me back to my hotel. The ride was a projected traffic-filled thirty minutes but I didn’t mind at all because I knew I would just be chillin and gazing out the window. “RelaxiTaxi!” (IYKYK)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163773)

Instead of window gazing though I asked Grok to pull up my favorite chess grandmaster Eric Hanson. His videos relax me and his chess is wonderful to watch. I’ve been a big fan of the Chessbrahs for many years.

Another great action packed day here in Austin and I’ll be heading out for a few hours of poker very soon.

If you missed day one and two you can check them out here.

Day one: https://stacker.news/items/1602995

Day two: https://stacker.news/items/1603699

Thanks for reading and following along!

items.title: I finally visited Pubkey in Washington DC
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/162019)

I am attending a reunion of sorts of some old friends in DC.  I had some free time yesterday, so I finally got the opportunity to visit the Washington Pubkey.

I have posted a few times about the NYC version. I have a great time whenever I go:

https://stacker.news/items/219987/r/siggy47

https://stacker.news/items/230440/r/siggy47

https://stacker.news/items/1283387/r/siggy47

The Washington DC version of Pubkey is located on 7th Street in the [Penn Quarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Quarter) neighborhood of the city. It's not far from Ford's Theater and the J Edgar Hoover FBI building.  Capital One Arena, where the Washington Capitals play, is down the block. It is an upscale, touristy location.

Pubkey DC opened in January, 2026, according to the website, but I thought it had been around longer.  Yesterday the Washington Capitals had an early game, so there were plenty of fans in jerseys milling about. When I walked in I immediately noticed how different this place was from the New York version. It's huge, around 12,000 square feet, with two bars, a stage, and big screens everywhere showing sporting events. There was a good crowd, which looked to be a mix of tourists, locals, and hockey fans. I can't be certain, but I'm pretty sure I was the only person in the place interested in bitcoin.

This is not an in your face bitcoin space. I had just had a long car and was hungry. I decided to sit at the bar and have some lunch after exploring a bit.

At first I didn't notice much bitcoin stuff, but it is all strategically placed to fit in unobtrusively. I liked the low key design. It could be any sports /tourist spot in any city.

There were a few stickers in the men's room:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162028)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162029)

I then noticed a large wall display with some actively mining bitaxes:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162030)

And this small, but intriguing stack of bitcoin and bitcoin adjacent books below a "Free Samourai" sign:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162032)

I sat at the bar and saw this cool display:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162033)

Occasionally the ticker had a news flash scrolling across the screen.

When ordering my lunch I let the bartender know that I planned to pay in bitcoin. I was told that if I did, I would receive a 21% discount, which is impressive. I asked about the payment setup, and was a little disappointed that they just use square. I tried to.engage my server in a little bitcoin banter, but it was obvious he had no deep interest. I dont want to sound negative. All of the workers were friendly and competent. The menu was similar to the NYC Pubkey. I had a Caesar wrap, which was very good.  I must say paying with the square app was quick and easy. You select the tip amount before the invoice is generated, which is nice. I have experienced a few awkward moments trying to tip at the NYC Pubkey. You never can be sure if the server would prefer sats or dollars. This way they probably get a choice.

That being said, paying with square is still disappointing.

On the way out I found this board near the front bar:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162036)

I guess this proves there are some bitcoiners patronizing the place.

I didn't get to experience an event, but there is plenty of room for bitcoin gatherings. NYC Pubkey always feels a little cramped. I know Thomas Massie will be holding a discussion soon. I hope I get some time on my next trip to catch a presentation.

items.title: Bitpost P2P
items.text:
Why should we have to wait for online stores to accept Bitcoin before we can actually use it? ⚡

Millions of people shop online every day, yet most e-commerce stores still don't accept Bitcoin.

But what if the solution isn't convincing merchants to accept Bitcoin, but changing the way we shop?

That's the idea behind Bitpost.

We've built a peer-to-peer marketplace that connects two types of people:

🟠 People who want to spend Bitcoin to buy products online.

🟠 People who want to stack Bitcoin by purchasing those products on someone else's behalf using traditional payment methods, and receiving BTC in return.

No merchant integrations required. No need for online stores to accept Bitcoin directly.

We started with Amazon to validate the concept, but our vision goes much further.

Our goal is to make Bitcoin spendable across any e-commerce store, without depending on merchants to adopt it.

Bitpost is already live in its first version.

We've seen strong interest from people who want to stack sats through this model.

Now we're looking for the other side: people who actually want to spend Bitcoin.

Because we believe Bitcoin shouldn't just be something you hold. It should also be something you have the freedom to use.

So here's our question for the Bitcoin community:

If you could shop at any online store using Bitcoin, even when that store doesn't accept BTC, would you?

And more importantly, what would make you trust and try a service like this?

We're genuinely interested in your ideas, concerns, and honest criticism.

🌐 https://www.bitpost.shop

The future of shopping with Bitcoin shouldn't have to wait for merchants to catch up.⚡
